title: India Asks UN Rights Office for Report on Pakistan's Actions in PoK
excerpt: First Secretary Anuj Swarup pressed the OHCHR at the UN General Assembly for a follow-up on killings, detentions and internet restrictions in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, accusing it of extreme selectivity.
body:
• India has asked the UN human rights office when it will issue a report on steps Pakistan has taken to address concerns in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, including investigations into killings and internet restrictions.
  • First Secretary Anuj Swarup delivered the demand at an interactive dialogue with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights at the 81st UN General Assembly's Third Committee.
  • India accused the OHCHR of "extreme selectivity," saying violent responses to protests elsewhere had gone uncommented.
  • The OHCHR had earlier called for impartial investigations into killings in PoK, due process for detained Joint Awami Action Committee leaders, and lifting of internet restrictions.

India has pressed the UN human rights office to say when it will report on Pakistan's handling of the situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), turning the body's own earlier statements into a demand for follow-through. First Secretary Anuj Swarup, of India's Permanent Mission to the UN, raised the question during an interactive dialogue with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly's Third Committee on Wednesday, according to India Today.

"When can we expect OHCHR to issue a report on the steps taken by the Government of Pakistan on this?"

— Anuj Swarup, First Secretary, Permanent Mission of India to the UN

What the UN rights office had said

Swarup referred to detailed OHCHR statements on PoK that called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations into killings allegedly carried out by armed and security forces. The statements also urged authorities to ensure detained leaders of the Joint Awami Action Committee had access to legal representation and their families, with due process and a fair trial, and called for internet restrictions across Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir to be lifted and meaningful political dialogue held.

The High Commissioner had noted that dozens of people — mostly protesters, but also law enforcement personnel — had reportedly been killed since June, ahead of the July 27 Legislative Assembly elections. India's question was pointed: having documented those concerns, when would the office report on what Pakistan had done about them?

"Extreme selectivity"

Swarup accused the OHCHR of "extreme selectivity" in addressing such incidents, as reported by 7Globe. "Violent responses to protests in our neighbourhood as well as in the west have gone uncommented. Needless to say, such double standards contribute to loss of trust in multilateralism and the work of OHCHR," he said. Pakistan, he added, "would do well to look inwards" and reflect on rights not being enjoyed in large parts of the country, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Rawalakot, which he described as under illegal occupation.

He said India's Constitution guarantees fundamental rights to every citizen, that law enforcement acts in accordance with the law, and that courts remain available for redress — and stressed that people in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh hold the same rights, both regions being integral and inalienable parts of India.

The wider exchange

The remarks came days after New Delhi described OHCHR comments on protests in the national capital as "unwarranted" and "unacceptable interference" in India's internal affairs, after the UN rights office expressed concern over reports of mass detentions of demonstrators and civil society members in Delhi. India said it would continue to engage with the High Commissioner and the OHCHR in a spirit of trust and partnership — "without selectivity and double standards."

What happens next

The ball is now in the OHCHR's court: whether it issues the follow-up report India demanded, and how it handles the selectivity charge, will test the credibility argument New Delhi is building at the UN. For Pakistan, the demand keeps international attention on the PoK unrest — the killings, detentions and internet restrictions its government has yet to publicly account for in a UN forum.
